findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Clarify AC5 to explicitly state which (if any) of the six ADR-listed monkeypatch targets move in this extraction — if none do, say so; if the except-spine creates a new patchable surface (e.g. `interpret_failure` itself), enumerate it.
evidence: ADR 0056 Consequences: 'Six string-keyed `monkeypatch.setattr(runner_mod, …)` targets move: `cache_settings_for`, `_pai_model` (×3), `_local_proxy_bypass_base_url`, `ProviderSession`, `_pai_structured`.'
Grep confirms none of these symbols appear in runner.py lines 555-629 (the except spine); they are all defined/re-exported at module-top or in pre-call code.
ABSENCE: the plan does not state 'zero of the six targets move in this extraction' nor does it enumerate any new targets that the except-spine extraction might create
findings.finding: AC5 says 'any monkeypatch target that moved is repointed IN THE SAME COMMIT … (see the parent's note on the six known targets)' without verifying which, if any, of the six targets actually live in the except spine being extracted. Confirmed: all six ADR-listed targets (`cache_settings_for`, `_pai_model`×3, `_local_proxy_bypass_base_url`, `ProviderSession`, `_pai_structured`) are pre-call/structured-run symbols, not in the except spine. The AC as written implies the implementer must consult an external document (the ADR) to determine scope, and may either do unnecessary repointing work or — if the extraction introduces a seventh target not in the ADR's list — miss it.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria, AC5; 'see the parent's note on the six known targets'
scenarios: An implementer reads AC5, consults the ADR, identifies all six targets, and spends time verifying none need repointing — wasted effort that a clear 'N/A for this ticket' statement would eliminate.
If the except-spine extraction causes a new symbol (e.g. `interpret_failure` itself) to become a monkeypatch target in existing tests, the plan provides no mechanism to catch it.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the cross-reference with an inline statement such as: 'None of the six pre-call monkeypatch targets (listed in ADR 0056 Consequences) move in this extraction. If `interpret_failure` is defined in a new module, verify no test patches it via `setattr(runner_mod, …)` before the commit.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the concrete attribute/field name for the disposition metadata in AC3 and add 'a test asserts the disposition is readable from `exc.<field>`' matching the pattern of AC1 and AC2.
evidence: AC1 and AC2 each say 'a test asserts …'; AC3 states a property but does not say 'a test asserts …' or name any proving command
'METADATA' is undefined — it could be an exception attribute, a dict, a dataclass field, or a side-channel; no attribute name is given
Without a field name, a test author cannot write a deterministic assertion
findings.finding: AC3 ('the classified disposition is still attached as METADATA') has no explicit test or proving command; 'METADATA' is not tied to a concrete attribute name, leaving the criterion unverifiable without inspecting the implementation.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria – AC3 ('the classified disposition is still attached as METADATA without changing the raised type')
scenarios: Implementer attaches the disposition under a different attribute name than reviewers expect; AC3 passes informally but the contract with callers is broken
CI never exercises the metadata attachment because no test targets it, allowing a silent regression
findings.suggested_fix: Revise AC3 to: 'a test asserts that after `interpret_failure()` the raised exception carries `exc.disposition` (or whichever attribute name is canonical) equal to the classified value, and that the raised type is unchanged.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add to the Scope section a description of how/where disposition metadata is attached (object, attribute name, point in the arm) so AC3 has a corresponding described deliverable.
evidence: Scope describes: 'src/rebar/llm/runner.py:507-581 -> interpret_failure(...) with explicit parameters' and 'Preserve the three arms\' ORDER'
AC3 states: 'the classified disposition is still attached as METADATA without changing the raised type'
No mention of metadata attachment mechanism, attribute name, or attachment site anywhere in Scope, Why, or Testing sections
findings.finding: AC3 ('the classified disposition is still attached as METADATA without changing the raised type') has no corresponding described work in the Scope section — the Scope only describes extracting the function and preserving arm order, never mentioning how or where disposition metadata is attached. This makes AC3 an orphan criterion: implementers have no specification to code against, and reviewers have no baseline to verify against.
scenarios: Implementer doesn't know which object carries the metadata, what attribute name to use, or at which point in the arm to attach it — they must infer from the existing code with no spec guidance.
A reviewer checking AC3 has no described behavior to compare against, so the AC cannot be verified against the plan.
findings.suggested_fix: In the Scope section, add a sentence such as: 'The extracted function must preserve the existing pattern of attaching the classified disposition as metadata on the exception instance (e.g., `exc.disposition = ...`) before re-raising, so callers inspecting that attribute continue to work.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Expand the Testing section description to explicitly include metadata-attachment assertions, so it is coherent with AC3 (e.g., 'verify disposition metadata is attached to the raised exception').
evidence: Testing section: 'Unit tier: pure given an exception and the counters'
AC3: 'the classified disposition is still attached as METADATA without changing the raised type'
Metadata attachment is not a counter or exception-type property — it requires inspecting an attribute on the raised exception
findings.finding: The Testing section ('Unit tier: pure given an exception and the counters') describes tests only in terms of exceptions and counters, but AC3 requires verifying metadata attachment — a behavior not captured by 'exception and the counters'. This is a cross-section contradiction: the testing strategy is narrower than the full set of ACs demands.
findings.location: Testing section vs. Acceptance Criteria AC3
scenarios: A developer reading only the Testing section may write tests covering only exception type and counter values, omitting AC3's metadata assertion entirely and shipping a passing-but-incomplete test suite.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the Testing section to: 'Unit tier: pure given an exception and the counters. Tests must assert (a) raised type, (b) arm ordering, and (c) disposition metadata attached to the exception.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an explicit rollback/back-out plan (e.g., 'revert this single commit; the extraction is atomic') or expand-contract sequencing so the reversibility mechanism is documented, not just the breakage acknowledgement.
evidence: AC2 acknowledges 'every existing `except LLMUnavailableError` caller keeps working'
AC5 acknowledges monkeypatch targets must be repointed 'IN THE SAME COMMIT'
No section describes what to do if the extraction is found to be broken post-merge (revert strategy, feature flag, expand-contract sequence)
findings.finding: The plan acknowledges caller-compatibility and monkeypatch-target concerns (AC2, AC5) but provides no explicit rollback/back-out plan or expand-contract sequencing if the extraction breaks something in production or CI. T4 requires the remedy to be a reversibility mechanism, not just acknowledgement.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria — AC2, AC5; plan as a whole
scenarios: If the extraction introduces a subtle behavioral difference caught only in integration or production, the team has no documented back-out plan — they must improvise a revert under pressure.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a 'Rollback' subsection: 'This extraction is a single atomic commit. If post-merge issues are found, revert the commit in its entirety; no data migration or schema change is involved, so revert is safe and immediate.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an AC (or expand AC2) to explicitly test the broad Exception arm's non-reclassification sub-path: when translate_sampling_parameter_rejection does not match the exception, assert the correct generic error type/behavior is produced and no exception is swallowed.
evidence: 'The broad arm tries translate_sampling_parameter_rejection FIRST; that ordering is load-bearing.'
AC1 only asserts the positive reclassification case ('is reclassified to the typed config error and NOT to LLMUnavailableError')
AC2 says 'raised TYPE is unchanged for each of the three arms' without distinguishing the two sub-paths of the broad arm
ABSENCE: no AC explicitly tests the non-reclassification fallthrough path of the broad arm
findings.finding: The broad Exception arm has two sub-paths — translate_sampling_parameter_rejection reclassifies (covered by AC1) and translate_sampling_parameter_rejection does NOT reclassify (falls through to the generic path) — but no AC explicitly targets the non-reclassification fallthrough. AC2's 'type is unchanged for each of the three arms' treats the broad arm as one case and does not distinguish these two sub-paths. A test is needed to confirm that when translate_sampling_parameter_rejection does not match, the fallthrough behavior (generic LLMUnavailableError or equivalent) is preserved and not accidentally dropped or misclassified.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria — AC1 and AC2; Scope note on translate_sampling_parameter_rejection ordering
scenarios: If a future edit changes the fallthrough behavior (e.g., accidentally swallows the exception or maps it to the wrong type), no AC directly catches the regression
The arm-ordering guarantee is incomplete if only the reclassification branch is tested — the complement (no match → correct generic behavior) is equally load-bearing
findings.suggested_fix: Add an AC: 'a test asserts that when the broad Exception arm's translate_sampling_parameter_rejection call does not match (returns None / leaves exception unchanged), the fallthrough produces the expected generic error classification and does not swallow or misclassify the exception.'
